interactionData.question: Which of these is a red flag in a scam message?

options.feedback: A friendly greeting alone isn't a red flag - scammers often use them to seem legitimate.
Correct! Urgent language is a classic scam tactic designed to make you act without thinking.
Professional formatting doesn't indicate a scam - in fact, many scams look very professional.
When a message is sent doesn't tell you if it's a scam or not.

coaching.onSuccess: Great job! You correctly identified the pressure tactic. Remember, legitimate businesses rarely create artificial urgency.
coaching.onPartialSuccess: You're getting there! Think about what tactics scammers use to rush you into action.
coaching.onFailure: Don't worry - this is a learning process. Scammers often use urgent language to make you act without thinking.
hints: Think about what makes you feel pressured
Scammers want you to act fast before you can think

sections.title: Test: Multi-Select Question
sections.body: This tests the 'select all that apply' feature with partial credit scoring.

interactionData.question:
Select ALL the red flags you see in this message:

> 'URGENT! Your bank account will be CLOSED in 1 hour! Click here to verify: http://bank-secure-login.xyz'

options.text: Uses urgent language (URGENT, CLOSED in 1 hour)
options.feedback: Yes! The all-caps 'URGENT' and impossibly short deadline are pressure tactics.

options.text: Suspicious link (xyz domain, not official bank)
options.feedback: Correct! The .xyz domain and 'bank-secure-login' are not from a real bank.
Right! Threatening consequences is a common scare tactic.
Messages about banking aren't automatically scams - it's the other elements that make this suspicious.

coaching.onSuccess: Excellent! You identified all the key red flags. You're developing strong scam detection skills!
coaching.onPartialSuccess: Good work finding some red flags! Review the ones you missed to strengthen your awareness.
coaching.onFailure: That's okay - spotting multiple red flags takes practice. Let's review what makes this message suspicious.
hints: Look at the language - is it creating pressure?
Check the link - does it look like a real bank URL?

finalQuiz.question: What should you do FIRST when you receive a suspicious message?

options.feedback: Never click links in suspicious messages - they could lead to phishing sites or malware.

options.text: Pause and look for red flags
options.feedback: Correct! Pausing gives you time to think and spot warning signs before taking any action.
Replying confirms your number is active and could lead to more scam attempts.
